A Jingdezhen porcelain bowl and box mysteriously shattered inside a display case at the British Museum , and when photos spread on social media, so did questions about their preservation and a perceived lack of attention around the incident, reports Artforum and the South China Morning Post . The museum confirmed the incident occurred on October 4 but found no signs to explain how a three-hundred-year-old bowl could have fallen onto a box below, breaking both objects, which are now being repaired. Chinese visitors posted photographs of the broken pieces in the display, which “has sparked debate on Chinese social media over how museums should protect fragile works,” reported SCMP .

The Digest

In a speech at the opening ceremony celebrating the newly expanded Kunsthalle Würth in the German town of Schwäbisch Hall, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier warned of nationalist threats to the “freedom of art,” referencing institutions such as the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation museum and design center, which “fears for its survival.” [ dpa ] Art Cologne, an art fair founded in 1967, is moving to a new, more spacious venue in Hall 1 of the Confex Conference and Exhibition Center , starting with the October 2027 edition. Donald Insall , an architect and “pioneering conservationist,” who notably worked on renovating and preserving Windsor Castle after it was damaged in a 1992 fire, has died at age 100, his studio announced. [ Dezeen ]

Meet Invictibellatrix amberina , a newly discovered cousin of the Tyrannosaurus rex whose fossil was uncovered on the Isle of Wight. Better yet, the new name partly means “unconquered female warrior.” [ Times of London ]

In a first, Israel returned 22 antiquities to Greece amid the latter government’s campaign to restitute missing parts of the Acropolis that were removed and placed in museums around the world, including the Parthenon Marbles . [ The Associated Press ]

Archaeologists have just uncovered the oldest-known shipwreck off the Turkish coast, dating to between 4,400 and 4,700 years ago, or around the time that Egypt’s Great Pyramid of Giza was built, reports Independent and the Journal of Maritime Archaeology . Researchers found double-handled ceramic containers and stone anchors that would have been carried in what was likely a wooden trade ship, the remains of which have long vanished. “The three-holed stone anchors found in the wreck area resemble those seen in Bronze Age Minoan, Cypriot, Anatolian, Levantine contexts,” stated researchers, who noted these details could reveal new information about Bronze Age shipping techniques.

article_text:
Source: James Veysey/Shutterstock

Noel Clarke

UK actor and filmmaker Noel Clarke has pleaded not guilty to sex offences against five women as his trial began today (October 21) at Westminster Magistrates’ Court.

Clarke, 50, is accused of two counts of sexual assault, three of voyeurism, and one of exposure between 2007 and 2016. The offences are alleged to have taken place in London and Dorset.

The trial will move to Southwark Crown Court in November.

The charges followed an investigation that began in September 2025. The previous month, Clarke had lost the libel case he brought against Guardian News and Media for its reporting of sexual assault allegations against him from April 2021 onwards. This is the first time Clarke has been on trial.

Clarke’s credits include the films Kidulthood and Adulthood , and the series Doctor Who.

Speaking in September, detective superintendent Mike Cagney said: “The women connected to these charges continue to receive support from specially trained officers. We urge anyone who has been a victim of sexual assault to contact police. The information you provide will be dealt with in the utmost sensitivity, and we have trained investigators on hand to support you.”

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and that it is in the public interest to do so,” said Bethan David, deputy chief crown prosecutor for CPS London.

article_text:
The new Liam Neeson thriller “ The Mongoose ” is one of the actor’s best genre vehicles since “ Taken ” made him one of the world’s biggest action stars almost 20 years ago. Fast, funny, and often surprising in its emotional delicacy and depth, the story of a falsely accused special forces vet leading cops on a high speed pursuit has both some of the best set pieces of Neeson’s career (particularly the climactic helicopter chase) and one of his loosest, most relaxed performances. He seems to be having a really good time, and the positive vibes are infectious.

That Neeson is so comfortable in “The Mongoose” probably has something to do with the director at the helm, Mark Vanselow . “The Mongoose” is Vanselow’s feature directorial debut, but he’s hardly a newcomer — as a stunt performer, stunt coordinator, and second unit director, he’s racked up over a hundred credits. More than 30 of those are on films he made with Neeson, who he first met when he doubled the actor in 1998 on “Gun Shy.”

Since then, Vanselow has been Neeson’s stunt double (and in many cases, stunt coordinator and more) on over 30 films, including last year’s “The Naked Gun” — another movie that found Neeson in a refreshingly hilarious and relaxed mode. Vanselow credits Neeson with encouraging and supporting him as he moved into new positions over the years, and with fighting to get him on overseas productions like the “Taken” movies where it would have been easier for producers to hire locally.

“Liam was really instrumental in fighting for me every step of the way,” Vanselow said. “As I transitioned from stunt performer to other jobs, he almost saw those attributes in me before I did.” Together, Neeson and Vanselow tried not to settle into established ways of doing things, often finding new ways to stage action that required battles with filmmakers and financiers more comfortable with the status quo — luckily, Vanselow taking the reins as director meant that he and Neeson could try anything they wanted to on “The Mongoose” without fear.

It also meant they could work more efficiently. “ A lot of times, as a stunt coordinator or second unit director you’re trying to act on the director’s vision,” Vanselow said. “And then you’re in a situation where you might not have had time to talk about that, and you’ve got to decide, ‘What do I think the director’s going to want here?’ So we’ll shoot in multiple angles to give them more material to work with. But as the director you get to say, ‘I don’t need to have that — but I need that .'”

By carefully planning the movie with his department heads, Vanselow was able to shoot “The Mongoose” in 35 days, a tight schedule given the movie’s scale and ambition. One key factor was reuniting with cinematographer Tom Stern, who Vanselow and Neeson had worked with before and who got used to working quickly during his days with Clint Eastwood. “With Tom, you’re not waiting to go, it’s just there,” Vanselow said. “He’s a magician with these images, and you don’t have to wait.”

Vanselow was careful to take full advantage of prep to get everyone on the same page. “We worked really hard to keep everybody pulling on the rope in the same direction,” Vanselow said. “Sometimes you work on a film and it feels like everybody’s going in different directions, and having been in that position I worked really hard to be clear about what we were doing.”

That clarity was essential not only given the speed of the shoot but the challenge of the location, as “The Mongoose” doubled Australia for the U.S. “First of all, in a car movie, all the steering wheels are on the wrong side,” Vanselow said. As part of prep, Vanselow drove the exact route Neeson’s character drives in the U.S. and shot footage of every stop along the way. He gave the material to his production designer and other collaborators, enabling them to find locations in Australia that worked as convincing facsimiles.

Coordinating all of his department heads and units in prep allowed Vanselow to focus more intensely on performance during the actual shoot, which paid off not only in terms of Neeson’s work but that of the supporting cast. One of the real pleasures of “The Mongoose” is how stacked the ensemble is, with fine contributions from Marisa Tomei, Ving Rhames, Michael Chiklis, and other actors who match Neeson’s enthusiasm and intensity. For Vanselow, who began as an actor himself, working on dialogue scenes isn’t all that different from staging stunts.

“Fight choreography is just non-verbal dialogue,” Vanselow said. “You approach it the same way. I really wanted to do a character-driven story, and we worked on peeling it like an onion. At first, it looks like it’s just a car chase, and that gets you into the theater. As you dive deeper there’s a little more going on, so that it’s not just action for action’s sake. The action supports those stories. I just tried to create an environment where the actors could do the best work possible.”

“The Mongoose” opens in theaters on Friday, October 30.

article_text:
Queere Kulturschaffende in Istanbul unter Druck, Frieze Week in London und die meistgefälschten Künstler der Kunstgeschichte: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Mittwoch

Kunstszene

Einst galt Istanbul als Zentrum einer lebendigen Kunstszene, heute prägen Angst und staatliche Repression den Alltag queerer Kulturschaffender . In der "taz " beschreibt Ingo Arend die jüngsten Razzien gegen LGBTQI+-Vereine, Bars und Organisationen unter dem Motto "Wir sichern die Familie" als bislang härtesten Schlag seit der gewaltsamen Niederschlagung der Pride 2015. Ein geplantes Justizpaket soll auch queere Symbole in Kunst und Kultur verbieten. Viele Kulturschaffende schweigen oder verlassen das Land. "Es herrscht einmal mehr Finsternis am Bosporus", kommentiert Arend. Der inhaftierte Menschenrechtsaktivist Yıldız Tar warnt vor der politischen Instrumentalisierung der Queerfeindlichkeit: "Die größte Falle, vor der die Opposition in der Türkei steht, ist die Angst. Wir dürfen nicht in die Falle der Angst tappen."

Kunstmarkt

Im "Art Journal" fragt Tom Seymour, ob die Frieze Week in London tatsächlich Marktvertrauen zeigt oder es nur inszeniert. Er verweist auf drohende Steuererhöhungen vor dem Haushalt am 28. Oktober und auf abwandernde Milliardäre. Von den Auktionen, etwa Mondrians "Composition III" mit einer Schätzung bis zu 30 Millionen Pfund, erwartet er nur begrenzte Aussagekraft. Sein Fazit: Die Frieze Week könne "ein Publikum anziehen und ihm eine verdammt gute Zeit bieten", doch der Londoner Markt sei "weniger gefestigt, als seine jazz hands uns glauben machen".

Kunstgeschichte

Von Corot über Dalí bis Basquiat: In "ArtNews" beleuchtet Karen Chernik die Geschichte der meistgefälschten Künstler . Schätzungen zufolge bestehe etwa die Hälfte des Sekundärkunstmarkts aus Fälschungen und Fehlzuschreibungen. Manche Künstler wie Giorgio de Chirico hätten sogar eigene Werke rückdatiert und als vermeintlich ältere Originale verkauft. Andere, etwa Salvador Dalí, erleichterten Fälschern das Geschäft, indem sie Tausende Blankoblätter für spätere Drucke signierten. Auch Andy Warhols Marilyn-Monroe-Bilder und Basquiats Werke seien besonders betroffen. Zur Echtheitsprüfung dienten vor allem drei Kriterien: stilistische Analyse, Provenienz und naturwissenschaftliche Untersuchungen. Doch selbst Museen seien nicht vor Fehlurteilen gefeit, wie die spätere Wiederanerkennung eines Velázquez-Gemäldes zeige.

In der "New York Times" erzählt Linda Laban die Geschichte eines lange verborgenen Wandbilds von Keith Haring , das heute Teil eines für 25 Millionen Dollar angebotenen Luxus-Lofts in Manhattan ist. Der Künstler malte das Werk 1979 als Student der School of Visual Arts in einem ehemaligen Handelsgebäude in TriBeCa. Nachdem dort ein Restaurant eingezogen war, verschwand das Wandbild jahrzehntelang hinter Gipskarton und wurde erst 2007 wiederentdeckt. Es sei erstaunlich, "dass es zugedeckt war und niemand wusste, dass es da war", sagt der heutige Eigentümer Adam Zoia, der das Werk von der Keith Haring Foundation authentifizieren ließ. Die Kunsthändlerin Jenn Singer betont die historische Bedeutung: "Die Vorstellung, zufällig mit einem Haring zu leben", sei bemerkenswert. Das Wandbild ist mit Säulen, Trägern, Decke und Wänden fest verbunden und lässt sich nicht entfernen. "Jeder zukünftige Eigentümer dieses Raums wird zu seinem Hüter", sagt Singer. Das Werk sei "im wahrsten Sinne unbezahlbar", allein weil es überhaupt erhalten geblieben sei.

Das besondere Kunstwerk

SWR Kultur beschreibt den neuen Pavillon für Anselm Kiefers monumentales Gemälde "Schwarze Flocken" in Künzelsau als gelungenes Zusammenspiel von Architektur und Kunst. Der vom Architekten David Chipperfield entworfene Betonquader beherbergt ausschließlich das elf Meter hohe, sieben Meter breite Werk von 2007, das auf Paul Celans gleichnamiges Gedicht Bezug nimmt und Erfahrungen des Holocaust reflektiert. Von außen wirke der Bau wie "eine riesige aufrecht stehende graue Kiste", im Inneren sei es jedoch unglaublich hell". Sechs Deckenöffnungen lenken das Tageslicht so, dass die Technik kaum wahrnehmbar ist. Auch baulich sei der Pavillon ungewöhnlich: Eine rund 60 Zentimeter starke Konstruktion aus Beton, Ziegeln und Lehm sorgt für ein stabiles Raumklima, ohne dass Heizungs- oder Lüftungstechnik nötig wäre. Reporter Andreas Langen spricht von einer "wirklich sakralen, konzentrierten Atmosphäre". Als Chipperfield den Raum gesehen habe, habe er gesagt: "Oh, wie eine Kirche." Das Gebäude sei "wie auf den Leib geschneidert" und schaffe einen eigenen Resonanzraum für Kiefers Bild.

Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 NYFF coverage. The film arrives in theaters on November 6.

Blockbuster films in America often have faceless, nameless enemies. Villainous, fictional countries attempt to rule the world, steal nuclear codes, or set off a bioweapon, only to be taken down by one of our aging Hollywood stars. Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus Zero , the director’s sequel to 2023’s acclaimed Godzilla Minus One , takes a different approach. Its villains range from the American military (and government) to the kaiju Ghidorah, both of which are destructive. The geopolitical underpinnings of the film work as a reminder of what war causes and continues to cause. But it’s still a Godzilla movie, and Yamazaki scales up the action to blaring, symphonic proportions.

Set two years after the first film, Godzilla Minus Zero finds Japan largely dealing with the wreckage of WWII after atomic decimation at the hands of the United States. Many of the same actors return, the disaster-response crew again facing a kaiju. The team—response director Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), and pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki)—must face off with King Ghidorah, a giant, flying beast capable of ruining cities once it opens its mouth.

Yamazaki, who also wrote the film and did its visual effects, doesn’t turn away from carnage. Unlike many other blockbusters, his film looks directly at the destruction and death caused by wartime violence. Minus Zero ‘s pain is visceral. The camera lingers on the injured, the dying, the dead, forcing us to understand the consequences of American actions. These characters haven’t just been through fighting Godzilla; they’ve been fighting and recovering for the past decade.

The story shifts into two threads (a family drama and a heart-racing monster thriller) after the team fully understands the kaiju they’re facing. Yamazaki decides to spend time with the Shikishima trio, following Kōichi, his wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani) in the aftermath of her interaction with Godzilla. The family becomes the core of Minus Zero , further earning emotional beats of the third act as the faces of unending violence.

But this is Godzilla and Ghidorah’s movie. It’s a kaiju film with big action—planes flying overhead, monsters in the air and on the ground. Yamazaki does an incredible job framing the scope of the action, using myriad stationed characters to show the complexity of battling these creatures. Even as the film expands, it attempts and often succeeds at retaining humanity. Yamazaki always finds time to see how these people are reacting, how they are persevering. The kaiju themselves are breathtaking, applause-inducing, and just enormous.

Yoshioka, Murakami, and Hamabe bring pathos to the monster mash: these characters grapple with the past and present alike, each bringing a unique weight to this story. Yamazaki has made a Godzilla film that encapsulates destruction and resilience staged at a massive scale and is necessary to see in a packed theater.

Godzilla Minus Zero premiered at the 64th New York Film Festival and opens on November 6.

article_text:
Das geht fast in Richtung Kollektiv: Documenta-Leiterin Naomi Beckwith hat neue Mitglieder in ihr kuratorisches Team für die 16. Ausgabe der Kasseler Ausstellung berufen

Laut einer Mitteilung vom heutigen Donnerstag werden Raven Chacon, Osei Bonsu, Timea Junghaus und Noam Segal das kuratorische Team der Documenta Sixteen verstärken, die im Juni 2027 in Kassel beginnt. Damit nimmt die kommende Weltkunstschau zumindest in Sachen Personal immer weiter Gestalt an. Das kuratorische Kernteam um die künstlerische D16-Leiterin Naomi Beckwith ist schon länger bekannt und besteht aus Carla Acevedo-Yates , Romi Crawford , Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro und Xiaoyu Weng.

"I ch freue mich sehr, mit diesen brillanten Denker*innen und künstlerischen Akteur*innen zusammenzuarbeiten, deren Werte und Überzeugungen ebenso stark sind wie ihr Engagement für eine kollaborative Praxis", wird Beckwith zitiert. Die Vize-Direktorin des New Yorker Guggenheim-Museums wird zwar offiziell als alleinige Leiterin der Documenta geführt, hat aber schon mehrfach betont, dass ihr gemeinschaftliches Arbeiten am Herzen liegt und sie eine Documenta als Teamaufgabe sieht. In diesem Punkt ist sie gar nicht so weit vom indonesischen Kollektiv Ruangrupa entfernt, das 2022 die Documenta Fifteen verantwortete. Allerdings soll der Begriff des Kuratierens nach dem Antisemitismus-Eklat von 2022 wieder strenger interpretiert werden.

Raven Chacon ist ein US-amerikanischer Komponist und Künstler vom Stamm der Navajo. 2022 wurde er als erster indigener Künstler mit dem Pulitzer-Preis für Musik ausgezeichnet. Im Kunstverein Hannover war im vergangenen Jahr seine Einzelausstellung "Conductus" zu sehen .

Die Kuratorin Noam Segal interessiert sich für die Verbindungen von zeitgenössischer Kunst, Technologie und Gesellschaft und arbeitet wie Naomi Beckwith am Guggenheim-Museum in New York. 2022 war sie Teil des kuratorischen Teams der 12. Berlin-Biennale.

Timea Junghaus ist Kunsthistorikerin und Kuratorin und setzt sich unter anderem für die Rechte und Sichtbarkeit von Sinti und Roma ein. Sie ist Mitinitiatorin der Initiative RomaMoMA, die 2022 auf der Documenta Fifteen vertreten war. 2007 kuratierte sie den ersten Roma-Pavillon auf der 52. Biennale von Venedig.

Osei Bonsu ist bei der Londoner Tate Modern unter anderem für das internationale Programm und die Sammlungsstrategie verantwortlich. Sein Schwerpunkt liegt nach Angaben der Documenta auf "postkolonialen Ansätzen der Geschichtsschreibung und der Entwicklung globaler und transnationaler Modernismen, mit besonderem Blick auf Künstler*innen aus Afrika und dem Globalen Süden."

Die Documenta Sixteen eröffnet am 12. Juni 2027 in Kassel.

article_text:
愛知県の豊田市美術館で10月24日から「没後20年 井田照一展」が始まります。1960年代より次々と実験的な版画作品を発表し、独自の地位を確立した井田照一（1941─2006）。その創作活動は版画にとどまらず、油彩や水彩、立体、インスタレーションなど広範にわたりました。作家の没後20年を機に開催する本展では、豊田市美術館所蔵の初期から晩年の作品を通して、多領域に拡大していった作家の活動を振り返ります。

没後20年 井田照一展

会場：豊田市美術館（ 愛知県豊田市小坂本町8丁目5番地1 ）

会期：2026年10月24日（土）～ 2027年1月24日（ 日）

休館日：月曜日（ただし、11月23日、1月11日は開館）、休館日 12月28日～1月4日

開場時間：10時〜17時30分（入場は17時まで）

観覧料：当日窓展販売：一般1,300円、高校・大学生1,000円、中学生以下無料 オンライン販売：一般1,100円、高校・大学生800円、中学生以下無料 ※前売券及び20名以上の団体は当日料金から200円割引 ◆同時開催の長谷川繁展も見られるお得なセット券(オンライン限定) 一般2,000円、高校・大学生1,500円 ※高校・大学生の方は、学生証をご提示ください。

詳しくは 同館公式ホームページ へ。

コンセプト「表面は間である」

1960年代には独特なフォルムと鮮やかな色彩の版画で注目を集めた井田は、薄紙や紗布に図像を刷り、何層も重ねる試みを経て、1970年代半ばには紙の両面に図像を刷る表現にいたりました。版と紙（垂直の力と水平面）が出会う場を表面とするコンセプト「Surface is the Between（表面は間である）」はその後、井田の幅広い作品群へと昇華されていきます。

独自の版画、穴をも穿つ

豊田市美術館では2004年に回顧展「井田照一 版画の思考」を開催し、版画を軸に初期作品から最新作までを紹介しました。作家の没後20年を機に開催する本展では、井田照一の多彩な版画はもとより、初公開作品を含む油彩、水彩、ペーパーワーク、陶、ブロンズ、布のほかさまざまなメディアによる作品も多数展示します。垂直の力と水平面が出会う場としての版画だけではなく、重力により紙の表面に窪みや穴を物理的に穿ち、ブロンズや陶の表面を圧し、または内部を抉ることで新たな表面を生み出すなど、 作家の行為が時間軸にそって変化する面の重層として生まれる作品と対峙したとき、仮想と架空が日ごと色濃くなる現代に生きる私たちは何を見出すでしょう。 豊田市美術館所蔵の初期から晩年までの作品を通して、多領域に拡大していった作家の活動をあらためて振り返ります。

《Tantra》－有限の画面に広がる無限の宇宙

そして今回、作家の生きた軌跡ともいうべき作品《Tantra》の全点展示をおこないます。井田がまだ学生だった1962年から亡くなる2006年まで制作を続けた401点からなる《Tantra》は、定まった矩形と円が描かれた支持体に、水彩やグワッシュ、リトグラフなどとともに、骨や石、種、綿花、涙、煙など多種多様な素材を用いたミクストメディア作品です。常に変化していく自らを確認するように残された一点一点が井田の無限の思考そのものです。

無限に変化していく自らを確認するために必要な行為として、井田は日記のように《Tantra》を制作しました。

《Tantra》の全点展示は、活力にあふれた青年期から、病のなか制作に打ち込んだ最晩年まで、井田自らによる「人生の図解」を目にする貴重な機会です。

本展は、垂直と水平との間に生み出された多様な作品世界に来場者が触れ、奇才・井田照一の思考について思いをはせる機会となることでしょう。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ）

article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Sundance coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 16.

Picture this: it’s an overcast day in August 1972. You’re at a cocktail party at Duke Ellington’s townhouse in Harlem. As you awkwardly hold your glass of punch, you’re drowned in cacophonous conversation about art, politics, and society during one of the most vibrant intellectual and creative movements of the modern era. This is the experience of William and David Greaves’ Once Upon a Time in Harlem , an immersive and masterfully rendered documentary that presents a living, breathing oral history of the Harlem Renaissance. Watching it feels like unearthing treasure.

The party was organized by filmmaker William Greaves, who invited artists and intellectuals of the period to reflect on and interrogate their experiences while he captures it all with 16mm. The project was left unfinished at the time of William Greaves’ death in 2014, but his family endeavored to complete the film, and it’s safe to say he would be proud of their efforts. His son David, who was one of the camera operators at the event, has done a marvelous job inheriting direction.

The handheld footage and lively editing reproduces the energy of being at a bustling cocktail party, bouncing from one conversation to another, hearing a snippet of one interaction before being pulled into a larger discussion. The two-dozen-or-so contemporaries, some of whom haven’t seen each other in half a century, reflect on the storied period in the early 20th century with invigorating candor and spontaneity. They remember and honor; they debate and contest with arguments that reach a simmer but never boil over. There’s debate over the very concept of a retrospective as well as issues with the contemporary political vocabulary. And when things get too chaotic, William Greaves can be heard off-camera directing the conversation back to the topics at hand.

Like any artistic movement, parameters and meaning are fraught and contentious. Poet Arna Bontemps describes the period as “a prism reflecting all of the Black experience from the beginnings to the present.” In a one-on-one interview, Bontemps recites his poem “The Day-Breakers,” which he wrote about the very same people he was rubbing elbows with that day. If there’s anyone that steals the show, it’s painter, writer, and self-described dilettante Richard Bruce Nugent, who can always be found quite easily in his red turtleneck. (A deliberate choice? We’ll never know.) Nugent offers the nugget that while one lives through a period, they don’t think about it from a greater historical context and so there’s not much for him to say—a sentiment he undercuts as the film goes on.

David Greaves moves meticulously from the larger party to these smaller conversations, at times utilizing split-screens, while offering context for the conversations via archival footage. As the photographer James van der Zee plucks a few notes on Duke Ellington’s piano, we’re treated to selections of his photography that provide a contemporaneous look at the neighborhood’s denizens before cutting back to the same subjects, albeit with a few more wrinkles and greys.

The decision to hold the gathering at Ellington’s townhouse is an inspired choice (Ellington himself does not appear in the film). The stately space is a reflection of the importance and exploits of those populating it. At any given moment, you’ll have four or five living monuments of the era cradled in the frame by Ellington’s trophies and plaques. A more vital choice was when to hold this shindig. Everyone in attendance is well-spirited but also quite elderly. Langston Hughes, perhaps among the better-known names of the period, had died in 1967. The actor Leigh Whipper, who founded the Negro Actors Guild, made it to the party despite being in his 90s. If there was ever a time to get these people together, 1972 was a good call.

What results is a dense document of cultural history that includes just as many names of those not in attendance as there are on the guest list. I find it hard to believe anyone will walk away from Once Upon a Time in Harlem without a roster of people and work to Google upon getting home. Whether it’s the Modernist art of Aaron Douglas, the poetry of Countee Cullen, the aviator Herbert “The Black Eagle” Julien, or—my personal favorite—the mobster Casper Holstein, who used his less-than-scrupulous wealth to support much of the work produced at that time.

Van der Zee describes the event as “miles and miles of memories,” and the Greaves family clearly has much more they could have included. Thankfully, like any respectable movie, there’s bonus footage over the credits.

Once Upon a Time in Harlem premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “ You Can See Everything .”

Everybody’s talking about the A24 documentary “ You Can See Everything,” and many Oscar prognosticators are jumping on board the Best Picture bandwagon . Don’t buy the hype.

While there’s a lot to admire about Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s entertaining nonfiction approach to parsing the distorted reality of disgraced Thanatos founder Elizabeth Holmes just before she went to prison, it’s still a long road for a surprise box-office documentary hit ($45 million domestic and counting) to garner enough Oscar votes for a Best Picture nomination.

The folks who believe it’s possible are listening to the current buzz and noise, much of it from younger movie fans on social media, and the film ‘s undeniable heat. A24’s brilliant “no spoilers” marketing campaign has pushed more moviegoers than usual into theaters early in the run. But the Academy membership is still senior-centric.

Here are the necessary steps for A24 to nab a BP nod.

Step One: Critic group wins. This week’s Gotham nomination for Best Documentary Feature is a start. The movie needs to land awards from the NYFCC, LAFCA, and NSFC. The Golden Globes will be no help, as they do not give a documentary prize. Critic support will add prestige and convince laggards to watch the movie on the Academy portal.

Step Two: Lure international voters. “YCSE” is an American movie, even if it confronts alternate reality issues familiar to everyone. It has yet to open overseas. Recognition from the European Film Awards or BAFTAs would show support outside North America. (Checking on eligibility)

Step Three: Legitimize the movie with the 750-member documentary branch, which is notorious for rejecting popular nonfiction like Morgan Neville’s “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?” and Brett Morgen’s “Jane.” Some doc voters harbor strong opinions about reenactments, which YCSE leans into in the second half. There’s a strong chance the doc branch will not nominate this movie.

Step Four: Figure Out Nathan Fielder. The offbeat, deliberately awkward creator behind TV series “The Rehearsal” and “The Curse” is an acquired taste. He’s been doing some press interviews and panels, but full-court glad-handing may not be his strong suit.

Step Five: Break out of the doc box. In the Oscars ‘ 98-year history, no documentary has ever been nominated for Best Picture. Over the past two decades, none of the docs that have succeeded at the box office have made it, not even Michael Moore’s 2004 Palme d’Or winner “Fahrenheit 9/11” — which was ineligible for the Oscar because it played on TV before the contentious national election. Moore received two documentary Oscar nominations for “Sicko” and “Bowling for Columbine,” winning the prize for the latter.

Step Six: Beat out the A24 competition. Four movies are vying for Best Picture this year from A24. The distributor is also pushing Olivia Wilde’s four-hander “The Invite,” Jesse Eisenberg’s crowdpleaser “The Debut,” and rookie Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” (a more likely Original Screenplay nod). “No one has the bandwidth to do every film justice,” said one Oscar campaigner. “It’s hard for a studio to get more than two.”

Step Seven: Woo the actors. With more than 1,100 voters, the actors are the dominant branch in the Academy. On GoldDerby.com, Experts list Amanda Seyfried in the sixth spot as a Supporting Actor contender. (The movie is ranked eighth for Best Picture.) In “YCSE,” she performs transcripts as Elizabeth Holmes in various reenactments, whom she played in the TV series “The Dropout.” And she plays herself. This is a hard one to call. Many believe this is more about A24 hype than reality.

Step Eight: Do the Numbers. Look at branches of the Academy and count the ones that are likely to vote for this movie. The classic way of figuring out a Best Picture contender is to see where its support lies among the active 10,365 voters. That’s how I figured out that “F1” might make it to Best Picture last year. Some of the 750 documentary branch members will vote for “YCSE” and are the most likely to see the movie. Anyone can vote for Best Picture, but the doc is unlikely to win any craft nominations: animation (729), casting directors (191), cinematographers (326), costume designers (205), editors (421), hair & makeup (225), music (430), production design (446), production and technology (424, they don’t have a branch but they vote), short films (234), sound (575), and visual effects (679). More likely to vote for the movie are such non-crafts as artists representatives (266), directors (587), executives (770), marketing and public relations (672), producers (692), and writers (534). The movie has no script per se. But writers may appreciate its ingenious structure and evolution.

Finally, if “YCSE” were to become the first doc to score a Best Picture slot, it would likely do so without any other nominations.

Films and events

Cult

Godzilla Minus Zero

The sequel to Takashi Yamazaki’s acclaimed 2023 film is a true cinematic spectacle that’s sure to grip fans of Godzilla, as well as newcomers to the franchise.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Takashi Yamazaki

With Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe

Japan 2026. 135min

Courtesy of Anime Limited

Language Japanese With English subtitles

Access information

Wednesday 14 October 17:30

Audio description

Friday 16 October 17:30

Audio description

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Japan, 1949. Pilot Kōichi, his wife Noriko and adoptive daughter Akiko are attempting from recover from Godzilla’s recent attacks. But just as everything seems settled, a new danger emerges. Meanwhile, at the bottom of the sea, something is stirring. The first Japanese film to be shot for IMAX, Godzilla Minus Zero combines high-octane thrills with more than a little heart.

Grace Barber-Plentie

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Hot Spot

The new film from the acclaimed director of The Silent Twins is a daring and distinctive sci-fi thriller set in a near-future society ruled by sentient AI.

Rogue Trooper

Duncan Jones brings the beloved 2000 AD comic strip to life with an all-guns-blazing sci-fi animation, about a soldier in a dystopian future who is sent on an impossible mission.

Wildwood

A forest inhabited by magical beings is the setting for this epic stop-motion saga from LAIKA Studios.

article_text:
国立科学博物館（東京・上野公園）で10月31日から2027年2月21日まで開催される特別展「生きものたちの性」は、コラボグッズとオリジナルグッズがそれぞれ面白いのです。主なところを探ってみましょう。

コラボグッズは「はじめまして松尾です」

スペシャルコラボクリエイターとして参加する人気アニメクリエイター「はじめまして松尾です」は、独自の発想から生まれるキャラクターと、不条理の中に物語性を織り込んだ映像表現で注目を集めています。生きものたちの多様な「性」のあり方を、ユーモアと創造性あふれる視点で表現しました。本展覧会のために描き起こしたビジュアルが商品になって登場します！

オリジナルグッズも思わずうなる

本展オリジナルのグッズも性を掘り下げました。ウニのポーチは、ぱかっと開くと生殖巣と殻の図柄が出てきました。

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: The screenwriter-forward Austin Film Festival has officially wrapped its 2026 edition, revealing its Audience Award winners and turning to plans for 2027, setting the opening of submissions for its Film and Script competition beginning next month.

Vincent Grashaw’s Bruton , the drama based on true story and starring Theo Rossi, Aya Cash, Tammy Blanchard and Tony Hale, won the Marquee Feature Audience Award, the fest said, while Vincent Lin’s Chopin took the Narrative Audience Award title. Alec C. Cohen’s Petunia , about a wild night with a sick cat, scored a special recognition prize in the Narrative category.

Related Stories

‘Bruton:’ Biopic About Man Who Briefly Escaped Prison During 10 Year Sentence Lands Sales Rep Ahead Of Locarno Debut

Austin Film Festival Announces Script & Film Competition Awards

See the full list of Audience Award winners below.

Watch on Deadline

Two pics that won competitive jury awards at this year’s fest — documentary short Buried Under Years of Dust and the digital series Matched — also won Audience Awards. Dust , from director Sophie Sartain and which traces the journey of Emily Grodin, a woman silenced by autism who finally finds her voice, will air on PBS’ Independent Lens in January.

Another Audience Award winner, the documentary feature Cradled By Grace , an Austin-produced documentary about jazz trumpeter Ephraim Owens, will air on PBS stations beginning in February.

AAF also has set plans for its 34th annual Festival & Writers Conference, which will take place October 14–21, 2027. Submissions for its Film and Script competitions open December 7.

The 2026 Writers Conference featured more than 200 panels, workshops, roundtables and pitch competition sessions, while the festival drew more than 35,000 attendees and showcased 199 films from 24 countries.

Below is the AFF Audience Award winners list.

MARQUEE FEATURE

Bruton (U.S.; U.S. premiere) Writer-director: Vincent Grashaw Cast: Theo Rossi, Aya Cash, Tammy Blanchard, Tony Hale A tragic accident leads Bryan Bruton on a wild and unforgettable experience within the Florida prison system.

NARRATIVE FEATURE

Chopin (U.S.; world premiere) Writer-director: Vincent Lin Cast: Eddie Liu, Violett Beane, Leon Dai, Min Wu A second-generation Taiwanese American returns to his small American hometown to reconnect with the workaholic father he barely knows.

NARRATIVE FEATURE – SPECIAL RECOGNITION

Petunia (U.S.; world premiere) Writer-director: Alec C. Cohen Cast: Charlie McDermott, Vanessa Marano, John Ross Bowie, Devon Werkheiser When their kitten falls ill, an impulsive photographer and his overworked girlfriend scramble through a chaotic night of dead-end vet visits, financial roadblocks, and emotional clashes as they fight to save their pet and their relationship.

DOCUMENTARY FEATURE

Cradled by Grace (U.S.; world premiere) Director: Vanessa Reiser Cast: Ephraim Owens, Peter Bay, Sam Lipman, Giveton Gelin As iconic Austin trumpeter Ephraim Owens and composer Sam Lipman undertake an ambitious collaboration uniting Ephraim’s jazz style with the Austin Symphony Orchestra, a health challenge requires them to confront new realities and limits.

COMEDY VANGUARD FEATURE

Christmas Pop-Up (U.S.; world premiere) Writer: Geena Pietromonaco Director: Molly Muse Cast: Geena Pietromonaco, Zach Gilford, Mano Agapion, Ayanna Berkshire Desperate for a fresh start, an unlucky-in-love set decorator takes a job designing a Christmas Eve pop-up for a jaded celebrity chef, hoping to escape her current hell, living with her ex and his new girlfriend, before he proposes on New Year’s Eve.

DARK MATTERS FEATURE

Frank Stein M.D. (Canada; world premiere) Writers: Rowen Kahn & Aidan Kahn Director: Rowen Kahn Cast: Rick Worthy, Rowen Kahn, Sarah Jeffery, Peter Kelamis After a freak accident, a brilliant young neurosurgeon must do the unthinkable: Bring his estranged, mad-scientist father back to life. From the Kahn Brothers comes a brainy comedy about fathers and sons, science and madness, and second chances.

ANIMATED SHORT

A Little Death (Denmark) Writer: Jonathan Rockefeller Directors: Leto Meade, Jonathan Rockefeller Cast: Nami Annette Gillet, John Sparkes Death’s patience is tested as his sweet and gentle apprentice appears incapable of the task, leading him to seek professional help from the most unlikely of places.

DOCUMENTARY SHORT

Buried Under Years of Dust (U.S.) Writer: Emily Grodin Director: Sophie Sartain Cast: Emily Grodin, Valerie Gilpeer, Tom Grodin, Marta Amaya How does someone go from not communicating for 25 years to narrating her life story? Buried Under Years of Dust traces the remarkable journey of Emily Grodin, a woman silenced by autism, who finally finds her voice… and has a lot to say.

NARRATIVE SHORT

The 65 th (U.S.) Writers: Lesley Paterson, Brian Bloom, Oscar Torres Director: Anthony Nardolillo Cast: Anthony Ramos, Ismael Cruz Cordova, JR Villareal, Luke Mitchell Korea, 1952.
